projects.title: HU-001C Handheld Game Machine
projects.summary: An '80s-style handheld game machine, soldered, assembled, and debugged from a kit.
projects.description: A DIY handheld gaming system built from the HU-001C Funny Game Machine kit. A programmed STC15F2K60S2 microcontroller reads five push buttons and drives an LED dot-matrix display, a three-digit numeric display, and a buzzer to run several retro-style games. Members identified parts, read the supplied circuit references, soldered the board, fit the clear case, and tested the finished system. The club assembled and tested an existing kit; PCB design and game firmware were outside this build's scope.
build: Identify components and check resistor value, IC socket notch, transistor orientation, and capacitor polarity
Assemble the battery holder and connect power leads with correct polarity
Solder the core components, then the buttons, buzzer, matrix sections, and numeric display
Solder the micro-USB connector and IC socket, then seat the microcontroller and button caps
Close the clear case, install batteries, and test controls, display, game switching, and sound
troubleshooting: Excess solder risking bridges: reheated, desoldered, and re-soldered with less
Incomplete through-hole joints: reflowed, reworking from the other side where needed
Battery pack initially missed: added afterward, matching polarity to PCB markings
Intermittent power: battery contact clips extended slightly for firmer contact

projects.title: Light-Activated LED & Buzzer Alarm
projects.summary: A 3 V light-sensing alarm that lights an LED and sounds a buzzer, with adjustable sensitivity.
projects.description: A 3 V light-activated alarm that detects changes in ambient light and responds with an LED and a buzzer. A 5516 photoresistor and 10 kΩ potentiometer set the bias on an 8050 NPN transistor; when light crosses the chosen threshold, Q1 pulls its collector low, lighting the LED and switching an 8550 PNP high-side transistor to sound the buzzer. Members went from a printed schematic and parts kit to a soldered, working PCB.
build: Match each component to its PCB reference designator and verify values and orientation
Solder resistors and low-profile parts first
Install the LDR, potentiometer, LED, transistors, buzzer, and battery leads
Inspect for cold joints, bridges, and reversed polarized parts, then trim leads
Final visual inspection before connecting the 3 V supply
troubleshooting: LED dimmer than expected: continuity-checked the whole PCB with a Fluke 17B
Several beginner solder joints reflowed and verified
Circuit worked after repairs; remaining dim LED identified as a likely defective part and kept as a teaching example

images.alt: Completed light-activated alarm PCB connected to a two-cell battery holder

projects.title: Hollow Hive Animatronic Pumpkin
projects._levelNote: TODO(Kaeden): level not stated in the report; confirm ADVANCED.
projects.summary: A reactive animatronic pumpkin with animated eyes, ultrasonic sensing, and Raspberry Pi to ESP32 motion control. First place, 2026 Halloween competition.
projects.description: Hollow Hive began as a reactive animatronic pumpkin for the Wire Lion 2026 Halloween competition, where it took first place. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W drives two round eye displays and reads an HC-SR04 distance sensor, then sends text commands over UART to an ESP32 that controls the leg and sway servos and the lift and head-spin motors. After the competition, the team reused the electronics in a standalone robot. At the last recorded test (October 29, 2026) the eyes, automatic startup, the Pi-to-ESP32 command link, and leg positioning were working; distance forwarding, face tracking on the Pi, and the lift encoder were still in progress.

specs.label: COMPUTE
specs.value: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (eyes, sensing, commands)

specs.label: DISPLAYS
specs.value: Two 1.28" GC9A01 round SPI displays, 240 × 240, 12.5 fps

specs.label: SENSING
specs.value: HC-SR04 ultrasonic; Camera Module 2 for face tracking (tested on laptop)

specs.label: MOTION
specs.value: ESP32 DevKit V1; two MG995 servos; two N20 encoder motors

specs.label: POWER
specs.value: 2S LiPo 7.4 V 2200 mAh, 12 V boost, 6 V buck, 10 A fuse; Pi on 5 V 2.5 A adapter

build: Assemble power with motors disconnected; measure the 12.0 V and 6.0 V rails and verify polarity and fuse
Start the Raspberry Pi and confirm both round displays animate after boot without undervoltage or Wi-Fi dropouts
Share ground, connect Pi TX (GPIO14, pin 8) to ESP32 RX2 (GPIO16), and send STAND, SIT, and STATUS
Confirm the servos reach the 7° stand and 133° sit setpoints with the mechanism clear
Add external pull-ups on lift encoder inputs GPIO34/35 and measure real travel counts
Run the ultrasonic script with its serial option and confirm DIST values reach the ESP32
Then validate camera tracking on the Pi, head spin, automatic wake, and continuous sway
troubleshooting: Pi lost Wi-Fi when powered from a laptop USB port: a 5 V, 2.5 A wall adapter fixed it
Commands reached the ESP32 but replies never reached the Pi: switched to one-way commands; a blank first line and filtering nonprintable characters fixed initial noise
Distance readings never reached the ESP32: send option, UART wiring, and port ownership still being traced
Leg STAND and SIT directions took two firmware revisions to get right
Lift encoder reported only two counts: GPIO34/35 have no internal pull-ups, so external 10 kΩ pull-ups are the next fix
Face tracking worked on a laptop with simulated displays but not yet on the Pi Zero 2 W

images.alt: The Hollow Hive animatronic pumpkin: a large orange 3D-printed pumpkin with two round display eyes and an ultrasonic sensor on top, on a workbench

System block diagram: camera, ultrasonic sensor and planned Wi-Fi CSI feed the Pi Zero 2 W, which drives the eye screens over SPI and sends UART commands to the ESP32, which controls two servos and two encoder motors through a TB6612FNG driver

Power diagram: 2S LiPo through a 10 A fuse and switch to a 12 V boost converter for the motor driver and a 6 V buck converter for the servos; a separate 5 V wall adapter powers the Pi, which powers the ESP32
